```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
# Bash chunks are a record of commands you ran in the Terminal. Knitting shows them but doesn't run them again.
knitr::opts_hooks$set(engine = function(options) {
  if (options$engine == "bash") options$eval <- FALSE
  options
})
```

Notes for [Workshop 1](https://mb5370.bioinformatics.guide/workshop1.html). Run the commands for this workshop in the Terminal, from inside the `command_line` folder:

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/command_line
pwd
```

Replace the text below each heading with your own notes. Copy each command you run into a bash chunk like the one above.

## Basic unix commands

Terminal expects commands in R, console expects unix commands. Notes on `pwd`, `ls`, `cd` and how unix commands are put together.

```{bash}
pwd 
```

(print working directory) This shows the path within the tree.

```{bash}
ls
```

This shows files and directories present in our location.

```{bash}
ls -l
```

Shows more information (-1 shows long format for each file/directory)

```{bash}
ls -lr
```

This will reverse sort what ls -l shows. -l and r are flags.

```{bash}
ls -l /usr
```

Instead of my directory we are now looking inside usr directory

"\~" is my home directory, contains this RStudio project.

```{bash}
mkdir 
```

This makes new directory.

To change directory:

```{bash}
cd ~/mb5370-workshops/command_line
```

"cd" for change directory, then insert the new directory. \~ is shortcut for home directory.

## Viewing and searching files

Notes on `cat`, `head`, `grep` and `man`.

```{bash}
cat 
```

Take a look at the file using cat

```{bash}
head
```

Shows the first 10 lines (useful for large files)

```{bash}
head -2
```

Shows first 2 lines

```{bash}
grep
```

globally search a regular expression and print.

Finds lines matching specific strings in files. Example: if you want to find the fasta header... use:

```{bash}
grep '^>' test.fasta
```

```{bash}
grep KDRNKKNSAK test.fasta
```

If you want to find a specific amino acid sequence.

grep has around 50 flags.

-i -\> case insensitive match

-n -\> report line number of matches

-c -\> count all files that contain the pattern

-w -\> match whole words only

## Sequence file formats

The table below contains my notes on the fasta and fastq formats.

**Table 1:** Comparing FASTA and FASTQ formats

| FASTA | FASTQ |
|----|----|
| Used for reference data. There are no quality scores so they are assumed to be correct, and they are used for nucleotides as well as protein data. | FASTQ files are most commonly used for "raw" reads from next generation sequencing experiments. Includes quality scores for every base. |
| The FASTA format consists of 1 or more entries, each of which consists of a header and a sequence. The title is one line, and begins with "\>". | Contains additional information about the reliability of each base (very large files). Line 1 shows the identifier which begins with an "\@". Line 2 shows the sequence, line 3 shows the description and starts with a "+", and line 4 shows quality scores. FASTQ is the standard format used for Illumina short reads, and long reads by Nanopore or PacBio sequencing. |
